evidence: Four out of five foods sold for toddlers in the United States are ultraprocessed

nary_nodes.label: Toddler Foods Fail Nutrition Standards
evidence: Nearly half of those items also failed to meet at least one nutritional benchmark for children set by the World Health Organization.

nary_nodes.label: Research on Toddler Foods
evidence: research that analyzed more than 2,700 products on grocery store shelves

nary_nodes.label: Parents' Grocery Store Experience Inquiry
evidence: “We wanted to know what parents were seeing when they went to the grocery store,”

nary_nodes.label: Over 80% Products Ultraprocessed
evidence: “The answer is over 80% of the products are ultraprocessed,”

nary_nodes.label: Products High in Sugar and Sodium
evidence: “Many of them are high in sugar, high in sodium, but parents really cannot tell that from just walking down the aisle.”

nary_nodes.label: Parents Cannot Discern Product Health
evidence: “parents really cannot tell that from just walking down the aisle.”

nary_nodes.label: WHO Nutritional Guidelines for Toddler Foods
evidence: Commercial foods marketed for children between 6 and 36 months should have no added sugar, artificial sweeteners or concentrated fruit juices, and limited saturated fats and sodium, according to the WHO Nutrient and Promotion Profile Model.

nary_nodes.label: Toddler Products Failing Sugar Standards are Ultraprocessed
evidence: “We found toddler products which failed to meet WHO standards on sugar were four times as likely to be ultraprocessed,”

nary_nodes.label: Presentation of Research Findings
evidence: presented the preliminary research findings on Sunday at the annual meeting of the American Society for Nutrition.

nary_nodes.label: Foods High in Sodium, Fat, Calories
evidence: “Almost a quarter of the foods were higher in sodium than is recommended, and some were high in fat and calorie dense,” she added. “These included organic foods.”

nary_nodes.label: Specific Foods High in Sugar
evidence: Fruit pouches and oat bars are examples of foods that were high in sugar

nary_nodes.label: Specific Foods High in Sodium and Fat
evidence: ready-to-eat mac and cheese bowls and turkey sausages were high in sodium and fat

nary_nodes.label: Specific Foods High in Sodium, Fat, Calories
evidence: peanut butter puffs were high in sodium, fat and calories

nary_nodes.label: Ultraprocessed Foods Crowd Out Healthy Options
evidence: “The problem isn’t just what’s in these high-sugar, high-salt ultraprocessed foods, it’s what they crowd out,”

nary_nodes.label: Reducing Neurotoxic Chemical Exposure
evidence: reducing babies’ exposures to neurotoxic chemicals

nary_nodes.label: Toddlers Eating Unhealthy Foods Eat Fewer Healthy Foods
evidence: “A toddler who fills up on fruit snacks, sweetened yogurt, crackers and snack bars is likely to eat fewer whole grains, vegetables, beans and other healthier foods,”

nary_nodes.label: First 1000 Days Vital for Child Development
evidence: The first 1,000 days of a child’s life are vital for the growth and development of their brain and subsequent health

nary_nodes.label: Taste Preferences Set in Early Childhood
evidence: Early childhood is also the time when taste preferences are set for life

nary_nodes.label: Unhealthy Childhood Diet Leads to Poor Adult Choices
evidence: Eating too many overly sweet, highly processed foods in childhood may lead to choosing sugar and artificial flavors over natural, nutrient-dense foods in the years to come.

nary_nodes.label: Parents Not Limited to Toddler Aisle
evidence: “Parents don’t have to be on the baby and toddler aisle at the store once their kid is able to chew,”

nary_nodes.label: Kids Can Eat Family's Healthy Food
evidence: “Kids can eat whatever healthy foods and snacks the family is eating — just chop or mash it up,”

nary_nodes.label: Industry Misrepresents Toddler Food Health
evidence: “Industry has marketed these toddler foods to make parents believe these foods were created for the health of toddlers, and it’s just not true.”

nary_nodes.label: FDA Proposed Labeling Rule
evidence: The US Food and Drug Administration proposed a rule in 2025 for a mandatory, front-of-package labeling system for most packaged foods

nary_nodes.label: Toddler Foods Exempt from FDA Labeling Rule
evidence: foods marketed to children under 4 would be exempt from that requirement.

nary_nodes.label: Industry Offers Safe, Affordable Products
evidence: “America’s trusted household brands offer parents and caregivers a wide variety of safe, affordable and convenient product choices to meet different dietary needs, preferences and family budgets.”

nary_nodes.label: No Universal Definition of Ultraprocessed Food
evidence: There is currently no universally accepted scientific definition of the term ‘ultraprocessed’ food

nary_nodes.label: Cherry-Picking Data Undermines Science
evidence: “Cherry-picking data to fit a narrative undermines the seriousness of the need for risk-based, peer-reviewed and rigorous scientific processes.”

nary_nodes.label: Food Photography for Research
evidence: Hudson and her team photographed foods marketed to children between 6 and 36 months at 21 grocery stores in Austin, Texas.

nary_nodes.label: Excluded Foods from Study
evidence: First foods, such as infant formula, drinks and purees, were excluded from the study.

nary_nodes.label: Nutrition Label Analysis
evidence: Researchers analyzed nutrition labels on 2,783 products for grams of sugar, salt, saturated and unsaturated fat, total calories and additives.

nary_nodes.label: NOVA Classification Comparison
evidence: They then compared foods to the NOVA classification system, which separates foods into four categories based on the level of processing.

nary_nodes.label: NOVA Group One Definition
evidence: Group one of the NOVA system covers unprocessed or minimally processed foods in their natural state, such as fruits, vegetables, meat, milk and eggs.

nary_nodes.label: NOVA Group Two Definition
evidence: Group two includes culinary ingredients such as salt, herbs and oils.

nary_nodes.label: NOVA Group Three Definition
evidence: Group three consists of processed foods that combine groups one and two — canned goods and frozen vegetables are examples.

nary_nodes.label: NOVA Group Four Definition
evidence: Group four includes ultraprocessed foods, which typically contain artificial ingredients not found in whole foods. Additives include preservatives to resist mold and bacteria; emulsifiers to keep incompatible ingredients from separating; artificial colorings and dyes; fragrance and flavor enhancers; anti-foaming, bulking, bleaching, gelling and glazing agents; and added or altered sugar, salt and fats designed to make food more appealing.

nary_nodes.label: Prior Research on Additives
evidence: Prior research published in January found over 70% of 651 baby and toddler foods contained additives that emerging research has linked to inflammation and disruptions in the gut microbiome.

nary_nodes.label: Baby/Toddler Foods Contain Harmful Additives
evidence: over 70% of 651 baby and toddler foods contained additives that emerging research has linked to inflammation and disruptions in the gut microbiome.

nary_nodes.label: Additives are Top Ingredient in Baby Foods
evidence: “What shocked me was the top ingredient in 71% of these baby foods wasn’t a fruit or vegetable — it was one or more additives,”

nary_nodes.label: Babies' Guts Cannot Handle Additives
evidence: “We know that babies’ guts are not fully developed enough to be able to handle additives in the way an adult stomach could,”

nary_nodes.label: Additives are Cosmetic, Not Necessary
evidence: “There is no need for these additives; they are simply cosmetic, designed to make the food look more appealing.”

nary_nodes.label: Parents' Burden to Find Healthy Choices
evidence: experts say the burden falls on parents to find the healthy choices among the lineup of less healthy products.

nary_nodes.label: Parents Must Read Labels
evidence: parents must read nutrition labels and ingredient lists

nary_nodes.label: Toddler Foods Not Necessarily Healthy
evidence: “You can’t assume foods marketed for toddlers are actually healthy,”

nary_nodes.label: 100% Fruit Pouch Can Have High Sugar
evidence: “A pouch labeled ‘100% fruit’ can deliver a big hit of sugar.”

nary_nodes.label: Snack for Little Fingers Can Be Unhealthy
evidence: “A snack that’s ‘perfect for little fingers’ can be loaded with artificial ingredients, too much salt, or industrial fatty acids.”

nary_nodes.label: Identify Unhealthy Foods by Labels
evidence: Look for “added sugar” and “saturated” fats on the nutrition label and if you see those, “put the food back on the shelf,” Hudson said. “Look at the additives in the ingredients at the bottom — are there natural and artificial flavors? Are there emulsifiers like gums, xanthan gum, carrageenan? All of these are markers of ultraprocessed or unhealthy foods.”

nary_nodes.label: Fruit Juice Concentrate is Hidden Sugar
evidence: Fruit juice concentrate is a red flag for hidden added sugars

nary_nodes.label: Fruit Juice Concentrates Lack Nutritive Value
evidence: “Fruit juice concentrates are essentially only the sugar and flavor of fruit — everything else with nutritive value has been stripped away, almost like a simple syrup,”

nary_nodes.label: Manufacturers Mislabel Fruit Juice Concentrate
evidence: “Sometimes manufacturers put fruit juice concentrate in the food and do not add it to the added sugars on the nutrition label even though that’s what it is.”

nary_nodes.label: Parents Should Prepare Healthy Foods at Home
evidence: parents should prepare healthy foods at home instead of using store-bought foods

nary_nodes.label: Limit Fruit Juice, Serve Whole Fruit
evidence: Try to limit fruit juice. Serve whole or diced fruit instead of pouches and purees.

nary_nodes.label: Guidance for Balanced Snacks
evidence: Pair fruit and veggies with protein and healthy fats like yogurt or nut butter — when age-appropriate — for balanced snacks. Offer lots of different fruits, vegetables, beans, healthy meats and whole grains.

nary_nodes.label: Parents Shouldn't Decode Packages
evidence: “Parents shouldn’t have to decode every package in the grocery store to find healthy food for toddlers,”

nary_nodes.label: Simpler Foods Best Until Stronger Standards
evidence: “But until stronger standards are in place, choosing and preparing simpler, less processed foods is one of the best ways to stack the odds in a toddler’s favor.”
